newsitem.title: UK: UK investigators still unravelling Sumitomo mystery.
newsitem.headline: UK investigators still unravelling Sumitomo mystery.

text.p: British fraud investigators are still unravelling the Sumitomo mystery one year after the giant Japanese conglomerate uncovered massive losses from rogue copper trading.
No one has been arrested in Britain, the global nerve-centre for metals trading.
And no-one expects a speedy conclusion to the probe.

Former Sumitomo star trader Yasuo Hamanaka is on trial in Japan after pleading guilty to fraud and forgery, but overseas investigations are trying to make sense of a tangled a web of deals spun by Hamanka which span the globe.
"It would be surprising if it took quicker. These big messy corporate cases always take a long time," said Michael Levi, professor of criminology at the University of Wales at Cardiff.
Serious Fraud Office (SFO) investigators have been sifting stacks of complex paperwork and working with their counterparts abroad, but they decline to say how close they are to any prosecutions.
"Cases would come to us only if they are very complex and so, inevitably, complex investigations take a long time," said SFO spokeswoman Ceinwen Jones.
"This is a large investigation involving considerable liaison with overseas jurisdictions," she added.

Industry sources still whisper of tangled conspiracies and hidden deals linking Tokyo, London and New York since Sumitomo announced on June 13 last year it had uncovered unauthorised trades that snowballed into $2.6 billion of losses.
Sumitomo says Hamanaka alone was responsible for the losses, which he kept hidden through forgery and other means.
British prosecutors may seek to bring charges of conspiracy to defraud or false accounting, but at the very least, they will first want to hear what Hamanaka says in his trial, Levi said.
"It's a question of what they can use and whether they can use him as a credible witness," he said.

Britain's Inland Revenue tax authorities said last month they met LME trading firms to discuss tax issues. Press reports have linked this meeting to the Sumitomo probe, but officials have not confirmed any relationship.
Little has been made public by the SFO, other than the fact it has made a handful of raids over the past year.

Press reports have said some of the searches were on premises belonging to the founders of the U.K.-based Winchester Commodities Group, Ashley Levett and Charles Vincent, but the SFO has declined to confirm this.
Winchester confirms it did business on behalf of Sumitomo, but strenuously denies any wrong-doing. The firm says it is co-operating with investigations.
The firm believes it has been unfairly singled out by the media since it says several other of the 19 brokerage firms and banks which handled Sumitomo business are also under investigation.

Japanese prosecutors said Winchester's local representative in Tokyo gave Hamanaka about 15 million yen ($132,000 at current exchange rates) in a gratitude payment. Winchester said the payment was made without the knowledge of Winchester or its shareholders.
Levett and Vincent, former floor traders on the London Metal Exchange, have relinquished their directorships in the company they founded in 1991 and now live in Monaco.
A British Broadcasting Corporation programme earlier this year put the spotlight on Winchester, alleging it charged Sumitomo inflated prices for a sophisticated copper deal.
But Winchester said its charges were fair for the 1993 deal, code-named RADR, which comprised more than 100 inter-related trades and was very risky.

The RADR deal was put together with the assistance of Credit Lyonnais Rouse, a ring dealing member of the London Metal Exchange, which was paid commission and took a share of 20 percent in any profit or loss, the BBC said.

Rouse, the London-based trading unit of the state-owned French bank, has denied any wrong-doing, but apologised after an LME investigation at the time, in case its involvement could have been interpreted as involving an undue influence over the market.
